nv_prince_of_darkness.notes: Shared with the neighbouring route. Small corners facing right lead up to a crack; the ground is easy enough that some parties solo it, others place a few pieces, to the bolted station.

A bolt line goes directly up the face. Holds are mostly incut edges, with a handful of slopers and moves that ask for balance. Ends at bolts. Some parties rate this the route's hardest pitch. When descending, use the rappel station off to the left, not this belay.
More of the same straight above, on edges and with plenty of bolts; a couple of pieces of gear fit the crack near the start. Ends at bolts.
Similar to the pitch below but slightly easier.
The angle eases toward slab, and the gaps between bolts grow in places. Ends at the station under the last pitch.

The crux comes immediately, between the belay and the second bolt. Incut edges give way to smooth slab split by a faint, shallow crack, taken on tiny holds and smears. The first bolt is a stretch, and falling before it can swing you onto the belayer. Higher up the edges come back, the difficulty drops, and the route finishes at a roomy ledge, the one belay on the climb where you are not hanging.

wa_beckey_tate.notes: Low-5th-class climbing up the obvious central ramp that splits the south face; easy ground used mainly to gain height and get established below the meat of the route.
Burly, slightly runout chimney climbing on rock that has a faintly unsettling, loose flavor typical of this face; bridge and stem rather than jamming to keep weight off suspect holds.
Good, positive climbing up a ramp-and-corner system to a belay slung off a tree above the ramp — one of the more straightforward pitches on the route.

Sustained chimney climbing where the gear (large #3/#4-size cams) sits far back in the crack, making the moves feel runout even though the pitch is technically protected; a fixed hex has been left in place at one of the harder placements — clip or back it up rather than relying on it alone.

The technical crux: the chimney above the previous belay resolves into a clean finger crack with secure, positive holds — reported as some of the best rock on the route, a welcome contrast to the looser climbing below.

A wavy hand crack/corner finishes the technical face pitches in excellent rock. From this belay a short scramble reaches the notch below the true summit; tagging it means joining the original 1942 West Face line for its last short pitches, ending in an exposed, essentially unprotected 5.6 slab move, guarded only by a single old 1/4-inch bolt most parties don't fully trust.
